Presenter: Our school is planning a responsible shopping fair. Where will the event take place next Saturday?
Noura: It will be held in the old market courtyard beside the town library.
Presenter: Why did the organisers choose a traditional souq instead of the new shopping centre?
Noura: Students want visitors to compare prices, meet local sellers and think about unnecessary waste.
Presenter: Will the stalls sell brand-new electronic products, or have the pupils prepared something different?
Noura: We are selling repaired lamps, reusable bags and notebooks made from leftover paper.
Presenter: Who repaired the lamps? Some visitors may worry that old electrical items are unsafe.
Noura: Each lamp was checked by a trained technician before it was accepted for sale.
Presenter: I heard your team invited younger pupils to help. What tasks can they safely perform?
Noura: They can label prices and welcome visitors, but teachers will supervise all payments.
Presenter: Is an entrance fee required? Families sometimes avoid events if admission is expensive.
Noura: Entrance is free. We want everyone to learn something about responsible buying.
Presenter: How will customers know whether a price has been reduced fairly or merely advertised attractively?
Noura: We will display the original price beside the reduced price and explain any discount.
Presenter: What should visitors do if they cannot understand the description of a product?
Noura: They should ask the seller for details instead of paying for something uncertain.
Presenter: Does every stall accept bank cards, or will some sellers use cash only?
Noura: Most will accept cash, and a teacher will record each sale in a shared register.
Presenter: Last year's posters showed an incorrect starting time. How did you prevent that mistake?
Noura: The final notice was checked by two teachers before it appeared on the school website.
Presenter: Some students think advertisements always tell the complete truth. How will the fair challenge that idea?
Noura: A small display compares persuasive slogans with clear descriptions of real product features.
Presenter: What will happen to useful items that remain unsold at the end of the afternoon?
Noura: They will be donated to a local community group, with permission from their makers.
Presenter: Will the volunteers keep the money raised, or is there a planned educational purpose?
Noura: The proceeds will buy basic equipment for our school's practical design club.
Presenter: How can a family help if they cannot buy anything during the fair?
Noura: They can share repair skills, bring clean reusable materials or simply attend a workshop.
Presenter: What do you hope pupils will remember when they see a tempting sale advertised online?
Noura: Compare evidence and prices, keep receipts and ask whether the purchase is truly necessary.

sections.script:
Part One

Last month, our class studied how advertisements influence shopping choices. I decided to examine a purchase I was planning to make. I needed a desk lamp because my old one was broken, and I had saved part of my pocket money for a replacement. On a shopping website, I saw a bright advertisement claiming that a modern lamp was twenty-five per cent cheaper than before. The photograph looked impressive, but the description did not clearly explain which accessories were included.

I ordered the lamp on Sunday, and the parcel arrived on Tuesday afternoon. I was excited until I opened the box. The lamp looked smaller than the photograph, and its charging cable was missing. I checked the online receipt and discovered that the seller had listed the cable as a separate purchase. I had overlooked that detail because the advertisement drew my attention to the discount rather than the full conditions.

Instead of posting an angry message immediately, I contacted customer service. The assistant was polite but explained that the missing cable was not included in the advertised price. She offered me a return under the shop's seven-day policy. I kept the packaging and saved our conversation so that I could make a careful decision.

Part Two

The next morning, our consumer-awareness teacher encouraged me to compare several local shops before deciding what to do. I visited a traditional souq with my older sister. A shopkeeper demonstrated two lamps, explained how much electricity they used, and showed us their warranties. One lamp cost a little more than the online offer, but the cable was included and replacement parts were available.

I returned the original lamp within seven days and received the amount I had paid. Then I bought the locally demonstrated lamp using my savings. It was not the cheapest option, but the total cost and conditions were clear. The experience made me realise that an advertisement can highlight a true fact while leaving out other details that matter to a customer.

For our class project, I presented both advertisements with their complete descriptions. We discussed how to recognise a persuasive slogan, compare a product's actual features and ask about the return policy before paying. Several classmates said they would now check the total price, including accessories and delivery, instead of trusting a large discount number.

Email 1 — From Amal to Green Market Online

Dear Customer Service Team,

Last Monday I ordered a study lamp from your website because the advertisement showed a significant discount. The description said the lamp could be charged by USB, and the photograph included a charging cable. My parcel arrived on Thursday, but the box contained no cable. The lamp itself seems undamaged. I checked the order confirmation, and I cannot find a sentence clearly explaining that the cable is sold separately.

I would like to know whether the missing cable can be supplied without an extra charge. If that is not possible, please explain the return procedure and whether I must pay delivery costs. I have kept the receipt, the packaging and a copy of the advertisement.

Kind regards,
Amal

Email 2 — From Customer Service to Amal

Dear Amal,

Thank you for explaining the problem clearly and sending the order number. We have reviewed your purchase. The USB cable is listed under optional accessories in the full product description, but we agree that our main photograph may have created a misleading impression. We will make the wording more obvious for future customers.

You may choose one of two options. We can send a compatible cable free of charge, or you may return the lamp within fourteen days of delivery. If you choose the return, we will provide a prepaid label and refund the original purchase price after the item has been checked. Please do not send the parcel before receiving the label.

Sincerely,
Green Market Online Support

Email 3 — From Amal to Customer Service

Dear Support Team,

Thank you for your prompt response. I appreciate your decision to improve the advertisement. I would prefer to receive the free cable because the lamp suits my desk and I do not want a working product to be wasted. Please confirm the delivery address already attached to my order and tell me when the cable is expected.

I will keep the original receipt and show your message to our school's consumer-awareness group. We are studying how clear descriptions and fair return policies can prevent misunderstandings. Your explanation will help us discuss both the customer's responsibilities and the seller's duties.

Best wishes,
Amal

sections.passage:
People often think that a low price automatically makes a purchase a good decision. In reality, responsible shopping involves several separate questions. A buyer should consider whether an item is needed, how long it may last, what the complete cost will be and what happens if the product develops a fault. These questions apply to traditional markets, shopping centres and online stores.

Advertisements can provide useful information, but their main purpose is often to persuade customers. A slogan might draw attention to a large discount without mentioning delivery fees or accessories that must be bought separately. Good shoppers therefore read the detailed description and compare similar products. They also recognise that an attractive photograph cannot demonstrate the quality of an item on its own.

A receipt is another important part of a purchase. It normally shows the date, amount paid and details of the product. Keeping a receipt helps a customer explain a problem accurately and may be necessary when asking for an exchange or refund. In an online transaction, the confirmation email can serve a similar purpose. Customers should save this information in a safe place rather than share private payment details publicly.

Consumers must also understand the difference between a warranty and a return policy. A warranty may explain what happens if a product stops working under certain conditions, while a return policy describes when the shop will accept an item back. The exact rules can differ, so assumptions based on another seller's policy may be unreliable. Asking a clear question before payment is usually easier than solving a misunderstanding afterwards.

Responsible shopping also has environmental and community benefits. Repairing an item, choosing durable materials or using a reusable bag can reduce unnecessary waste. Buying from a local seller may make it easier to inspect goods and ask about their origin, although local products are not automatically better in every situation. What matters is comparing evidence rather than relying on a single attractive claim.

Students can practise these skills by examining two advertisements for similar products. They can identify the essential features, calculate the total price and discuss which questions remain unanswered. Such exercises teach financial awareness and careful communication. The goal is not to avoid every purchase, but to make decisions that are informed, fair and suitable for a person's actual needs.

Every school can develop these habits through classroom discussions, consumer-awareness workshops and community projects that involve both families and students.

sections.script:
Part One

My name is Hamed, and last month I attended a university open day with two classmates. We wanted to compare different courses before submitting applications. Our teacher had advised us to prepare questions, so we made a list about entry requirements, practical training, library facilities and the cost of living away from home. We also agreed not to rely on comments from strangers online when checking important information.

The first session introduced students to the engineering department. A lecturer explained that the first year includes mathematics, laboratory work and group projects. She showed us a typical weekly timetable and reminded us that independent study requires planning. I was surprised to learn that students often work together to solve practical problems rather than study every subject alone. After the talk, we visited a workshop where older students demonstrated a simple water-saving device.

We then spoke with a student adviser. She explained how new students can ask for help with course choices, study methods and personal difficulties. She also suggested checking the official university website regularly because deadlines and entry requirements may change. I wrote down the contact details for the admissions office and asked whether scholarships were available. The adviser encouraged us to compare realistic costs, including transport and accommodation, before making a final decision.

Part Two

In the afternoon, we joined a guided tour of the library and study areas. The librarian showed us how to find reliable academic sources and book quiet rooms for group work. My friend Mariam asked whether students could borrow laptops, while Faisal wanted to know about accessible study spaces. The librarian explained that equipment and support services differ between institutions, so applicants should ask direct questions.

Before leaving, we attended a short discussion with current students. They described how they balanced lectures, revision, exercise and family commitments. One student said he had initially struggled with time management but improved after joining a study-skills workshop. Another explained that asking questions during tutorials helped her feel more confident. Their experiences were different, which reminded us that there is no single perfect way to adjust to university life.

On the journey home, we compared our notes and corrected a misunderstanding about one application deadline. I realised that an open day is useful not because it makes every decision for you, but because it helps you collect evidence and identify further questions. I now plan to speak with my family, review official course details and prepare a realistic budget before choosing where to apply.

Dear Mariam,

Thank you for asking about my first month at university. I was excited when I arrived, but the timetable was quite different from school. Some lectures finished early while others were followed by laboratory sessions, so I had to plan independent study rather than wait for homework instructions. I now keep a weekly schedule that includes revision, meals, exercise and time to contact my family. It is not perfect, but it helps me avoid leaving assignments until the final evening. I check it each Sunday and change my plan when a group project requires extra preparation.

You asked how I chose my course. Before applying, I compared the official descriptions of several programmes. I checked entry requirements, practical modules and the support available to first-year students. I also attended an open day and spoke to current students. Their experiences were different, so I did not assume that one person's opinion represented everyone. The admissions office answered a question about a deadline that had been reported incorrectly on social media.

Living away from home has taught me to manage money carefully. I record transport, food and study expenses, then review the totals every weekend. I still make mistakes, especially when I buy things without planning, but I am learning to make realistic choices. My roommate and I also share responsibility for keeping our study area tidy. We disagree occasionally, yet discussing expectations calmly has helped us work together. We have even agreed on quiet hours before important assessments.

If you are worried about making friends, remember that many new students feel uncertain. I joined a small science club, where we work on practical projects and discuss our interests. I also attended a study-skills workshop after finding my first research assignment difficult. The adviser showed us how to locate reliable sources and ask questions during tutorials.

Please do not think you must solve every problem alone. University independence means taking responsibility, but it also means knowing when to ask for help. I hope you can visit a campus before making your final choice. Write back and tell me which subjects interest you most.

Best wishes,
Salim

When Abdullah received an offer to study at university, he was pleased but nervous. He had worked hard at school, yet he had never lived away from his family. His first concern was accommodation. He compared the university residence with a rented room, checking costs, transport and the distance from lectures. After discussing the options with his parents, he chose the residence for the first semester.

During orientation week, Abdullah met students from different towns. Some were confident speaking to strangers, while others were quiet. He joined a small group exploring the library and science laboratories. A student guide explained how to borrow books, reserve study spaces and contact an academic adviser. Abdullah wrote down the information because he knew he would not remember every detail from the tour. He also learned where to find the official timetable and how to check changes to lecture rooms.

His first group assignment was more difficult than expected. Four students had to prepare a presentation about reducing water use on campus. Abdullah wanted to start collecting facts immediately, but another member suggested dividing the responsibilities first. They agreed that two people would research reliable sources, one would design the slides and Abdullah would organise the speaking order.

A week later, the team discovered that one of their figures came from an outdated report. The presentation was due soon, and Abdullah considered keeping the number to save time. His classmate reminded him that accurate information mattered more than finishing early. They checked the university library database, found a newer report and changed their conclusion. The extra work made the presentation clearer and more trustworthy.

At the same time, Abdullah struggled to balance lectures with independent study. He sometimes spent too long on his phone and then rushed through homework. After attending a study-skills workshop, he began using a weekly timetable with short breaks. He also started walking in the evenings and contacting his family regularly. These changes did not remove every difficulty, but they helped him feel more organised. His roommate encouraged him to keep trying even when a difficult week interrupted the new routine.

At the end of the semester, Abdullah realised that university independence did not mean solving every problem alone. He had learned to compare reliable information, discuss decisions, respect teammates and ask advisers for support when necessary. He was still learning, but he felt better prepared for the next stage of his studies.

sections.script:
Part One

My name is Noura, and I joined a visitor welcome programme because I wanted to understand how real services help different people. Our teacher encouraged us to learn from professionals rather than rely on a few pictures on the internet. The first meeting took place at the local heritage guesthouse. We discussed the importance of clear information and how visitors may have different needs, budgets and expectations.

Our team then spoke to hotel supervisor, who explained the ordinary responsibilities involved in this work. We prepared information cards and practised welcoming guests and explaining local customs. Some students enjoyed meeting new people, while others preferred checking facts or organising resources. The teacher reminded us that careful preparation is just as important as confident speaking. We kept a notebook recording decisions and the sources used to verify each important detail.

During our first trial we noticed an incorrectly recorded booking time. At first, one member suggested leaving the information unchanged because the deadline was near. I disagreed, and we checked the confirmed reservation before making a correction. We then informed the other students so they would not repeat the mistake. The experience showed that a small error may create real inconvenience for people who trust a service.

Part Two

A week later, we invited visiting families to test our explanations. Some participants requested clearer instructions while others asked about accessibility and practical arrangements. We listened carefully, considered their feedback and updated the materials where appropriate. We also learned to avoid making assumptions about a person's circumstances. Asking a respectful question was often the best way to understand what somebody actually needed.

The group discussed why responsible hospitality involves both professional knowledge and personal responsibility. We compared different ways of communicating and considered how changes should be announced promptly. Our teacher encouraged us to explain not just what we had changed but also why the original version had been confusing.

At the end of the project, I wrote a short reflection. I had gained confidence in working with a team and using reliable evidence. I understood that a successful activity is not measured only by the number of people who attend. It is also measured by whether the information is accurate, the service is respectful and people can make informed decisions.

It is to practise responsible judgement, cooperation and clear communication.

sections.script:
Part One

My name is Khalid, and I joined a student transport information project because I wanted to understand how real services help different people. Our teacher encouraged us to learn from professionals rather than rely on a few pictures on the internet. The first meeting took place at the town transport centre. We discussed the importance of clear information and how visitors may have different needs, budgets and expectations.

Our team then spoke to transport coordinator, who explained the ordinary responsibilities involved in this work. We prepared route maps and practised comparing routes and travel options. Some students enjoyed meeting new people, while others preferred checking facts or organising resources. The teacher reminded us that careful preparation is just as important as confident speaking. We kept a notebook recording decisions and the sources used to verify each important detail.

During our first trial we noticed an outdated bus departure time. At first, one member suggested leaving the information unchanged because the deadline was near. I disagreed, and we checked the official timetable before making a correction. We then informed the other students so they would not repeat the mistake. The experience showed that a small error may create real inconvenience for people who trust a service.

Part Two

A week later, we invited daily passengers to test our explanations. Some participants requested clearer instructions while others asked about accessibility and practical arrangements. We listened carefully, considered their feedback and updated the materials where appropriate. We also learned to avoid making assumptions about a person's circumstances. Asking a respectful question was often the best way to understand what somebody actually needed.

The group discussed why safer public transport involves both professional knowledge and personal responsibility. We compared different ways of communicating and considered how changes should be announced promptly. Our teacher encouraged us to explain not just what we had changed but also why the original version had been confusing.

At the end of the project, I wrote a short reflection. I had gained confidence in working with a team and using reliable evidence. I understood that a successful activity is not measured only by the number of people who attend. It is also measured by whether the information is accurate, the service is respectful and people can make informed decisions.
